seo.title: Karmic tail 9 3 3 compatibility: The Hermit and two Empresses
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 3 3 compatibility: The Hermit, two Empresses and The Devil at the couple's centre. Why the middle is 3, not 12, and which garden the couple must grow.

title: Karmic tail 9-3-3 in compatibility: a hut for two in someone else's garden
short: The couple's tail 9-3-3 looks like a misprint. By the personal formula, 12 would stand between The Hermit and The Empress, yet here the middle is The Empress again. The couple's story hides inside this oddity. Two people enter the union wanting to be alone together (9, The Hermit), live by growing a home and care (3, The Empress), and their main task is the same Empress taken seriously: to grow their own garden on their own ground, not to keep it secretly in someone else's house.

sections.h2: The first clue: a middle that no single person has
paragraphs: In a personal chart the tail is built as a chain: the middle equals the entry plus the main task. 9 and 3 would give 12, The Hanged Man, and a personal tail 9-12-3 does exist. A couple's tail works differently. Each of its points is found by adding the matching points of two personal charts and reducing the sum to 22. The couple's middle is not derived from its ends — it is added up from the partners' middles. So instead of The Hanged Man, who hangs and waits, the couple has The Empress in the middle, who grows.

The 9-3-3 has only one family tree. Running the site's engine through every date shows that this tail appears only in a couple where one partner's personal tail is 21-10-16 (The World, The Wheel of Fortune, The Tower) and the other's is 6-20-14 (The Lovers, Judgement, Temperance). There are no other combinations.

ul: **Entry:** The World 21 + The Lovers 6 = 27 → 2 + 7 = **9, The Hermit**.
**Middle:** The Wheel of Fortune 10 + Judgement 20 = 30 → **3, The Empress**.
**Main task:** The Tower 16 + Temperance 14 = 30 → **3, The Empress**.

paragraphs: Read these sums as sentences and they make a short story. The whole world plus a choice adds up to solitude for two. A turn of fate plus an inner call adds up to growth. Collapse plus measure adds up to growth again. Two different roads give the same sum, 30, and both lead to The Empress.

The tail is rare: it occurs in roughly one couple out of 3,171 (0.032%) and ranks 92nd of the 97 couple tails. It has no permutations: neither 3-9-3 nor 3-3-9 ever appears in a couple, so 9-3-3 is the only order of these numbers.

Every such couple has the same centre — 15, The Devil. The partner with the 21-10-16 tail always has a personal centre of 5 (The Hierophant), the partner with 6-20-14 always has 10 (The Wheel of Fortune), and 5 + 10 = 15. No date ever gives 15 at the centre of a personal chart: this card appears only when two people are added together. "The couple's values" hold The Hermit in 94.2% of cases and The Moon in 5.8%.

There is a subtler clue too. Benebell Wen assigns an element to each card. The partners' personal tails carry all four: for her The World is Earth, The Lovers Air, The Wheel, The Tower and Temperance Fire, and Judgement, by her choice, Water. Yet everything the couple ends up with — The Hermit, both Empresses, The Devil at the centre and The Hermit in the values — is, in Wen's words, a card that "the element of Earth governs". Out of two people's air, fire and water comes solid earth. Keep this in mind: in the story below, everything comes down to ground.

sections.h2: The story: "Six Records of a Floating Life"
paragraphs: In 1877 a manuscript was printed in Shanghai. The brother-in-law of the writer and publisher Wang Tao had found it at a stall selling second-hand books. Its author, Shen Fu of Suzhou, was born in 1763, worked as a private secretary to officials, traded and sold paintings. He was never famous. The manuscript was called "Six Records of a Floating Life" (浮生六記), but only four records survived: of wedded joys, of idle pleasures, of sorrows and of travels. The fifth and sixth are lost, and every "rediscovered" sequel turned out to be a forgery. In English it is available, among other versions, in the translation by Leonard Pratt and Chiang Su-hui (1983); the quotations below are our own translations from the Chinese.

Shen Fu opens by saying he has no intention of inventing anything: he merely records "true feelings and true events". The first record is entirely about his wife, Chen Yun, and their twenty-three years of marriage. For its time this was unusual: a husband writing about his wife as his closest friend, the one he shared books, jokes and outings with.

The title is a clue as well. The words "floating life" come from Li Bai, from his preface to poems about a spring feast in a garden: "Heaven and earth are an inn for the ten thousand things; time is a traveller passing through a hundred generations. And floating life is like a dream — how much joy is in it?" Li Bai was Yun's favourite poet. A book about a couple who spent their whole life in houses that were not theirs took its title from a line about an inn.
We do not know both partners' exact birth dates, and we do not assign the 9-3-3 tail to this couple. But their story can be read by these cards almost word for word.

sections.h2: The Hermit at the entry: porridge hidden for one
paragraphs: Shen Fu was thirteen when he told his mother: "If you are choosing a wife for me, I will have no one but Sister Shu." His mother slipped a gold ring off her finger, and the children were betrothed. That same winter, at the wedding of Yun's cousin, the boy grew hungry late at night. The maids brought him dried jujubes, too sweet. Then Yun secretly tugged at his sleeve and led him to her room. She had warm porridge and little side dishes hidden there. He had barely picked up his chopsticks when her cousin burst in: "I asked you for porridge just now and you said it was all gone. So you were hiding it for your bridegroom!" Yun burned with shame and fled, and the house roared with laughter. After that, whenever Shen Fu visited, he never saw her: she hid.
This is where the 9-3-3 tail begins: **care that is hidden from everyone except one person.** The porridge is The Empress, the hiding of it is The Hermit.

The second scene is the wedding, five years later. At supper the bride eats only meatless food, and Shen Fu realises she has kept a meatless vow for several years. He counts back the years: the vow began when he had smallpox. She had never said a word about it. "Now I am safe and sound — may my sister end her vow?" Yun answered with her eyes and a nod.

This is how the couple's common language worked. For twenty-three years, meeting in a dark room or a narrow passage, they would take each other's hand and ask, "Where are you going?" — hearts pounding as if someone might see. Yun, in her husband's words, could "read my eyes and understand my brows". They had their own jokes. Yun had taught herself to read from Bai Juyi's "Song of the Pipa", and called Li Taibai her favourite poet. Her husband laughed: Bai Juyi is your first teacher, Li Taibai your kindred spirit, and I, Sanbai, your husband — how lucky you are with the character 白, "white"! "I'm afraid I'll be writing nothing but 'white characters' from now on," Yun replied. In Suzhou "white characters" meant slips of the brush. Only the two of them got the joke.

This is no chance resemblance to the card. On the couple's chart, the point of entry to the tail is the very same point as "Common language" on the relationship line. Every 9-3-3 couple has The Hermit as its common language. Lisovskaya describes such a couple as if she had read this book: love here is shown by deeds rather than words, and other people hear about events once everything has already happened.

Today it looks like this. The couple has its own words that nobody else understands. One quietly pays the other's share and never mentions it. At a party they exchange a glance and both know it is time to go. The best weekends are the ones without guests. The family hears about plans once everything has been decided.

In Waite's list of divinatory meanings for The Hermit, "prudence, circumspection" stand beside "dissimulation". It is an uncomfortable word, yet it fits this couple exactly, except that here the pretence is kind. Yun tells her cousin there is no porridge left. She goes with her husband to Lake Tai, telling the household she is visiting her family. She dresses as a young man so she can see the flower festival at the temple with him. These are small screens with which two people fence off their "we" from the big house.
Wen offers another way to read The Hermit's lantern: someone "who sees the world through his or her own light", walks their own path and "is not a traditionalist". So was this marriage.

The entry stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish becomes resistance. When gossip started in the house, Yun forbade her husband to defend her: "Better that my father-in-law scold me than that I lose my mother-in-law's favour." And she never explained herself. **The silence that protected the two of them at first later leaves them without a voice.** Lisovskaya says it plainly in The Hermit's minus: problems pile up in silence.

sections.h2: The Empress in the middle: tea in a lotus flower
paragraphs: Shen Fu's second record is about how the couple lived, and all of it belongs to The Empress. Its last sentence is about tea. In summer, when lotuses are just beginning to bloom, they close at night and open in the morning. Yun would put a pinch of tea into a small silk bag and lower it into the heart of a flower. In the morning she took it out and brewed it with rainwater, and the fragrance was beyond compare.

This is the best image of the tail's middle: what is closed to everyone at night is steeped in fragrance by morning. The Hermit gives silence and closedness, The Empress turns them into fragrance and fruit.

Yun knew how to make plenty out of poverty. Her husband liked a drink with friends but disliked a crowd of side dishes, so Yun made a box in the shape of a plum blossom: six white dishes joined with lacquer into a single flower, "as if a plum blossom painted in ink had settled on the table". She sewed his caps and socks herself. In place of a railing on the veranda she hung an old bamboo blind. Her rule was called "deal with things as they are". Once, so that friends could drink hot tea among the flowering rapeseed, she hired a street seller of wontons together with his portable stove. "Without you none of this would have happened," the guests said.

Together they built a tiny mountain of stones on a tray. Vines grew on it, white water flowers bloomed around it, and the couple decided: "A pavilion over the water here, a thatched hut there. Here one could live, here fish, here gaze into the distance." Shen Fu writes that they talked as if they were about to move in. One night cats knocked the tray over, and both of them wept. The Hermit's hut, built by The Empress's hands, existed only on a tray.

For a 9-3-3 couple today the middle of the road looks much the same. Renovating a rented flat with their own hands, seedlings on the windowsill, Sunday lunches, a shared cat, a shared project. Their home turns warm out of almost nothing, and the two of them are happy in it.

But the same record contains a sentence that is easy to miss. Shen Fu explains why he puts cut chrysanthemums in vases instead of growing them in pots: **"our household had no garden, and I could not grow them myself."** Every garden this couple had belonged to someone else. The room by the Canglang Pavilion was in his father's house. The cottage by Jinmu Bridge was rented for a month. The tower where they were happiest was a friend's house. Then came the village house of Yun's sworn sister and two rented rooms in Yangzhou.

The book's best-known confession was made at Jinmu Bridge. An old woman let them a room in a cottage surrounded by vegetable plots. The neighbours, who lived by their gardens, brought fish and vegetables and refused money, so Yun made them shoes. Chrysanthemums were planted along the fence. And Yun said: "Some day we will build a house here. We'll buy ten mu of vegetable garden around it, the hired hands will grow melons and greens — enough for firewood and rice. You will paint, I will embroider — enough for poetry and wine. Cotton clothes and rice with vegetables — joy for a whole life, and no need to plan distant journeys." Shen Fu adds: "I agreed with all my heart. Now, even if such a place were found, my dearest friend is gone."
The whole tail is in that sentence. Solitude for two with a vegetable garden around it — 9 and 3 as a single wish. And the land that was never bought is the third card, the main task.

In The Empress reversed, Wen sees effort that bears no fruit and names the cause: **"The element of Earth is missing."** To succeed, the person "must commit to harnessing Earth qualities". This is where the solid earth into which this couple's elements add up comes in: it turns out to be the task.

sections.h2: The main task: whose garden is it?
paragraphs: Lisovskaya says the main task of a tail is read through its minus: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. For The Empress in this role, all the difficulties are earthly — family and money — and the lesson is grown-up practicality. Shen Fu's third record, "of sorrows", shows it in living people.

It opens with a saying: in family life nothing works without money. The couple had no money of its own. At first they pawned things and patched one hole with another, then they stopped making ends meet. The house began to whisper.

Shen Fu's father asked Yun to handle the family's letters. Her mother-in-law suspected her of writing the wrong things and took the letters away from her. The father decided Yun looked down on the job. Yun kept silent.

The father wished to take into service a woman from home, "so that our speech would match" — in effect, a concubine. The son wrote to his wife in secret, and Yun found a girl. While it was still unclear whether the match would work out, the mother-in-law was told that a neighbour's girl had come to play. When the truth came out, the mother-in-law turned against her daughter-in-law.

The brother-in-law borrowed money from a neighbour's wife and asked Yun to stand surety, and when the debt was called in, he claimed to know nothing. Yun wrote to her husband about it and, while she was at it, advised quietly persuading the concubine to say she was homesick. The father opened the letter and read that his wife was called in it "your honoured mother" and he himself "the old man". His verdict: "Your wife borrows behind her husband's back, slanders her brother-in-law, calls her mother-in-law 'your honoured mother' and her father-in-law 'the old man' — what outrage!" The couple was turned out of the house.

Put these stories together and a pattern emerges: **every misfortune in the third record grew out of hidden care.** A quiet note, a kindness done under a pretext, a surety nobody spoke of. There is a bitter detail too. Twelve years earlier Shen Fu had carved two seals with the words "to be husband and wife in life after life" — "for our letters to each other". The disaster came through a letter read by a third person. The language of two, read aloud in the elders' house, sounded like insolence.
Wen warns about this in The Hermit reversed: such a person "can be petulant to elders".

A few years later it happened again from the other side. Shen Fu stood surety for a friend who borrowed fifty taels of silver — it felt awkward to refuse. The friend vanished with the money, the lender shouted at the gate, and the father gave his son three days to move out.

In Lisovskaya's minus of The Hermit there is a line about money: such a couple needs someone to spur its material ambitions. In this couple Yun tried to be that person. When a relative invited Shen Fu to go trading in the south, saying he was "waiting for the dew to cook his rice", Yun backed him: "While your parents are still strong and you are young, better to work hard once than to count firewood and rice for ever." She packed her own embroidery and Suzhou wine-soaked crabs for him to sell.

The second time, they left at the fifth watch, before dawn, in secret, so that the neighbours would not laugh and the lender would not stop them. Before setting out they ate warm porridge. Yun, smiling with an effort, said: **"Once a bowl of porridge brought us together, now a bowl of porridge parts us. If anyone wrote a play about it, they could call it 'The Tale of the Porridge'."** The circle closed: the tail began with porridge hidden for one and ended with porridge eaten in secret before leaving someone else's house.

For a 9-3-3 couple today the main task looks mundane. The two live with one set of parents "until they've saved up", and the years go by. Decisions about the renovation are made by whoever owns the flat. One secretly borrows from a parent to plug a hole in the budget. The other signs as guarantor for a friend because refusing feels awkward. A joke the two of them share sounds rude in front of the family. And each time the couple hides instead of speaking.

The task is not to love less or to grow harder. It is for the garden to get ground of its own: their own budget, their own home, or at least their own rules where they live. Decisions made together and announced, not hidden. Money talked about before it runs short. And each partner with work of their own: Lisovskaya advises a couple with The Empress that each should find fulfilment separately.

sections.h2: The Devil at the centre: two people chained only to each other
paragraphs: The centre of the 9-3-3 tail is 15, and it is always made of 5 and 10: one partner's Hierophant and the other's Wheel of Fortune. The Hierophant is rite and rule, The Wheel a turn of fate. Together they give the card of being bound.

In "Six Records" there is a scene where this sum is all but spoken aloud. In the first months of marriage Yun was comically ceremonious: she thanked him for every trifle and rose to take a fan from his hand. Her husband lost patience: "Do you mean to bind me with ceremony?" She flushed: "Most quarrels in the world begin with jokes." They made peace, and from then on her "forgive me" and "how could I dare" turned into mere filler words between them. Rite tied to fate became a knot only the two of them understood.

Then came the seals. On the night of Qixi, the seventh night of the seventh moon, Shen Fu carved two seals with one inscription — "to be husband and wife in life after life". On his seal the characters were raised and printed red on white. On hers they were cut in and printed white on red. One vow in positive and negative.

Then Yun suggested they pray to Yue Lao, the Old Man under the Moon, the god of marriages. A painter they knew made his portrait: in one hand a red thread, in the other a staff with the book of marriages hanging from it. They hung it in their inner room and burned incense before it at every new and full moon. In the Tang tale that gave rise to this god, the old man reads his book by moonlight and carries a bag of red cords with which he ties the feet of future spouses. "Once this cord is tied, there is no escaping it."

Waite sees in The Devil "the chain and fatality of the material life", and in the divinatory list he adds a qualification: fatality is "that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". His book also has a detail that is easy to walk past. Describing older decks, he approves of Papus's version, in which the human figures on The Devil card are **"yoked only to each other"**: "The author may be felicitated on this improved symbolism." That is the centre of the 9-3-3 tail. No third party holds the chain; it is stretched between the two. The same goes for the centre 15: neither of the two has it alone, it appears only in the couple.

On the plus side, such a centre means strong attraction and the ability to accept the dark in the other. Shen Fu has a funny scene. Yun loved stinking fermented tofu and melon pickled in shrimp brine — things her husband loathed. He teased her: what are you, a dog or a cicada? Then she pushed a piece of the melon into his mouth with her chopsticks. He chewed holding his nose, then let go of it — and came to love it. Yun invented a sauce from the two pickles called "double freshness". "Where the heart is gathered, even the ugly does not repel," she said.

On the minus side, the same centre becomes a room without windows. That same night of Qixi, Yun looked at the moon and asked: "The universe is so vast, and there is one moon for all. Are there two other people in the world tonight who feel what we feel?" It is beautiful, and it is also the formula of "we need no one else".

In the spring of 1803, in two rented rooms in Yangzhou, shortly before the end, Yun told her husband: "Warm cotton clothes, a full meal of rice and vegetables, harmony in a single room, as at the Canglang Pavilion and in Xiaoshuang Lou — and we would be immortals among the hearth smoke… Strive for it by force, and you draw the Creator's envy and the turmoil of the demon of love." The demon of love (情魔) — that is what she herself called the force that held them and tormented them. Shen Fu drew his conclusion: spouses must not hate each other, but neither must they be too attached, for "loving couples do not last to the end together".

The cards disagree with that conclusion. Numbers say nothing about who will live how long or how long a union will last. Lisovskaya's final thought on The Devil in a couple is different: **nobody belongs to anybody.** There is no need to love less. What is needed is for love not to become a locked room. Shen Fu blames the depth of feeling, while the tail points to two other things — silence (9) and a garden without ground (3).

sections.h2: The strong version: a house with four prohibitions
paragraphs: This couple had a happy example too, and it grew out of a collapse. After the first expulsion, Shen Fu's friend, the painter Lu Banfang, took them into his tower, Xiaoshuang Lou — roughly "the Tower of Clear Coolness". They lived there for a year and a half. Shen Fu would later call them "immortals among the hearth smoke".

This is how they lived. Yun embroidered, the old maidservant spun, the manservant sewed clothes to sell — and that fed them. Friends knew their host was poor and brought "money on a staff". That was the name for chipping in for wine, ever since the poet Ruan Xiu hung a hundred coins on his staff on the way to the tavern. Yun cooked without spending: greens, fish and shrimp took on "an unexpected flavour" in her hands. When the wine ran short, she drew a hairpin from her hair — for wine — and her face did not change. The painters came, in Shen Fu's words, "like swallows under the rafters — flying in and out as they pleased".

The house had rules. Four prohibitions: talk of ranks and promotions, of office affairs, of official examination essays, of cards and dice. The fine for breaking one was five jin of wine. And four qualities that made a guest welcome: generosity, refinement, freedom from convention and **clear quiet**. The Hermit's silence remained — but as a virtue at a shared table, not as a wall.

This is the 9-3-3 tail in its plus, and it agrees with the numbers. The main task is made of The Tower and Temperance, collapse and measure. Here the couple's best home grew right after the expulsion and was held together by "dealing with things as they are". In Waite, The Hermit's lantern says: "where I am, you also may be." In Xiaoshuang Lou the hut for two gained a door.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the old man under the moon
paragraphs: In "The couple's values", 94.2% of 9-3-3 couples have The Hermit and the remaining 5.8% have The Moon. The Old Man under the Moon, to whom Shen Fu and Yun prayed, combines both cards: an old man with a staff and a book — and the moon he reads by. This is our observation, not the teaching of the books, but it shows where this couple looks for meaning: in quiet, in depth, in what not everyone can see.

The Hermit as a value has its shadow too. After his wife's death Shen Fu took the name Meiyi, roughly "plum recluse", in memory of the Song poet Lin Bu. Lin Bu lived alone on an island in a lake and never married, and people said of him: "the plum tree is his wife, the cranes his children". The solitude the two had dreamed of together was left to one.

There is light as well. Shen Fu wrote only "true feelings and true events". Almost seventy years later a stranger found his manuscript at a second-hand book stall, and since then the hidden life of two has become a lantern for strangers. For a 9-3-3 couple the value of The Hermit lies not in hiding the light but in carrying it.

A person born on 08.01.1976 has the personal karmic tail 6-20-14 and centre 10. A person born on 06.03.1978 has the tail 21-10-16 and centre 5. Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points, reduced to 22.
The middle is not recalculated from the ends: the personal formula would give 9 + 3 = 12, but the couple's middle is 20 + 10 = 30 → 3. "The couple's values" in this example are 9, The Hermit.

In this couple The Hermit also stands on the entire money line: "Way into money", "Path to prosperity" and "Where it leaks" are 9-9-9. Together with the entry to the tail (which is also "Common language") and the values, that makes five Hermits on one chart. But this belongs to the particular example, not to the tail: by our own count, the money line 9-9-9 occurs in 11.8% of 9-3-3 couples.

ul: **Don't hide the porridge.** Say care and sacrifices out loud: "I covered it", "I gave up the trip for us". Unseen kindness piles up in this couple and later turns into resentment.
**Ground of its own.** The couple's own budget, its own home, or at least its own rules where it lives. Decisions are made together and announced to the family, not cleared with the family in secret.
**Loans and sureties — only after talking it through together.** Both of Shen Fu and Yun's disasters had one cause: a signature nobody had agreed on.
**Translate the shared language for others.** A joke for two does not belong in a letter to the mother-in-law. Silence is for resting together, not for conversations about money.
**Open the door.** Invent a house with four prohibitions of its own: where friends come, where people are fed, and where the important things are discussed calmly.
**Nobody belongs to anybody.** Each partner needs work and time of their own. "We need no one else" is a lovely phrase and a poor plan.

**9 — The Hermit, "Entry to the task".** The couple's shared wish and its common language: quiet for two, understanding without words, care that is never put on show. The same wish turns into resistance when the important things go unsaid.

**3 — The Empress, "Middle of the task".** How the couple travels the path: it grows things. A home, comfort, housekeeping, shared projects, warmth for their own — all of it comes out of almost nothing.

**3 — The Empress, "Main task".** What there is to learn: to turn warmth into soil of their own. Their own home, their own money, their own decisions made without glancing at the family — and a garden other people can be invited into.

intro: Beneath the tail, every such couple has The Devil — a centre card that only a couple can have. In "The couple's values" The Hermit returns almost every time (94.2%). What follows is an investigation: clues in the numbers themselves, in Waite and Wen, and in a Chinese book about a marriage written more than two hundred years ago. Its love story begins with a hidden bowl of porridge.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 9-3-3 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task, not a verdict. At the entry is The Hermit: two people want quiet and solitude together and understand each other without words. In the middle and in the main task is The Empress: the couple grows a home and care, and what it has to learn is to set this garden on its own ground — its own money, its own decisions, its own home — and to keep it open to others.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the tail 3 and not 12?
faq.a: In a personal chart the middle equals the entry plus the main task, and 9 and 3 would give 12. In a couple's chart each point is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts: the middle is the sum of the partners' middles. For 9-3-3 that is always 10 + 20 = 30 → 3. That is why there is no personal 9-3-3 tail, while a couple can have one.

faq.q: Which personal tails add up to 9-3-3?
faq.a: Only one combination: one partner has the personal tail 21-10-16, the other 6-20-14. Running through the dates gives no other variants. This also fixes the couple's centre: personal centres 5 and 10 always add up to 15, The Devil.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a relationship?
faq.a: No. The tail shows where the couple stumbles and what it learns, but it does not predict events or dates. A 9-3-3 couple stumbles over silence and over living on someone else's territory, and grows when care becomes visible and the home becomes its own.

faq.q: Why does such a couple always have The Devil at the centre?
faq.a: Because the personal centres of partners with the tails 21-10-16 and 6-20-14 are always 5 and 10. No date gives 15 at the centre of a personal chart; it appears only in a couple. Its plus is strong attraction and acceptance of each other's dark sides, its lesson is that nobody belongs to anybody.

The whole 9-3-3 tail is already in it: **care that is hidden from everyone except one person.** The porridge is The Empress, the hiding of it is The Hermit.

report.h3: The silence that first protects, then takes away the voice

report.h3: A vegetable garden around a house that never existed

report: In the middle of the tail is The Empress: the couple grows things, and grows them out of almost nothing. What is closed to everyone at night is steeped in fragrance by morning — this is how The Hermit and The Empress work together in this couple.

Having rented a room for a month in a cottage among vegetable plots, Yun said: "Some day we will build a house here. We'll buy ten mu of vegetable garden around it… You will paint, I will embroider… Cotton clothes and rice with vegetables — joy for a whole life." Solitude and a vegetable garden, 9 and 3, are a single wish. Yet elsewhere in the same book Shen Fu lets slip: **"our household had no garden"**. Every garden this couple had belonged to someone else: his father's house, a rented room, a friend's tower.

So the main task is the same Empress read through its minus: family and money. The couple had no money of its own. Yun quietly handled things for others: she found her father-in-law a woman to serve him, telling her mother-in-law that a neighbour's girl had come to play; she stood surety for her brother-in-law. Her letter to her husband was opened by her father-in-law, who read in it "your honoured mother" and "the old man". The couple was turned out of the house. And twelve years earlier Shen Fu had carved two seals with the words "to be husband and wife in life after life" — "for our letters to each other". **Every misfortune grew out of hidden care**, and the language of two, read by the elders, sounded like insolence. A few years later Shen Fu, out of awkwardness, stood surety for a friend, the friend vanished with the money — and the couple was turned out again.

They left in secret, before dawn, and ate warm porridge before setting out. Yun, smiling with an effort, said: "Once a bowl of porridge brought us together, now a bowl of porridge parts us." The circle closed.

Today this task looks mundane. Two people live with parents for years, "until they've saved up". One secretly borrows from a parent, the other signs as guarantor because refusing feels awkward. There is one thing to learn: to give the garden ground of its own — its own budget, its own home, or at least its own rules where it lives, and decisions made together that are announced, not hidden.

Beneath the tail, such a couple has The Devil — a centre card that neither of the two has alone: it appears only when two people are added together. Waite, describing older decks, praises a version in which the human figures on The Devil card are **"yoked only to each other"**. Shen Fu and Yun prayed to the Old Man under the Moon, the god of marriages, who ties spouses together with a red thread: "Once this cord is tied, there is no escaping it."

On the plus side, such a chain means attraction and the ability to accept in the other even what one dislikes: Yun once pushed into her husband's mouth a pickle he loathed, and he came to love it. On the minus side, it is a room without windows: "Are there two other people in the world tonight who feel what we feel?"

Near the end, Yun herself called this force "the demon of love", and Shen Fu decided that the trouble lay in too strong an attachment. The cards disagree with that conclusion. The Devil's lesson in a couple is different: nobody belongs to anybody. There is no need to love less — what is needed is for love not to become a locked room.

report.h3: A hut that gained a door

report: This couple spent its best year and a half right after the first expulsion, in a friend's tower. Yun embroidered, guests chipped in for wine and came "like swallows under the rafters — flying in and out as they pleased". The house had four prohibitions — talk of ranks, of office affairs, of examinations and of cards and dice — and four qualities that made a guest welcome. The last of them was **clear quiet**. The Hermit's silence remained, but it became a virtue at a shared table rather than a wall.

The couple's best home grew out of a collapse and was held together by measure. In Waite, The Hermit's lantern promises that others can reach the place where he stands. The strong version of the 9-3-3 tail is a hut for two that has a door.
